Definition: Whether the system enables individuals to authenticate themselves or their documents digitally through electronic verification
Comments: The Houwiyeti app (launched 2023) and the e-ID system enable digital biometric authentication. Citizens can authenticate their identity digitally using facial biometrics (selfie) against their stored T5-Cryptograph digital ID for access to eGovernment services, replacing passwords with biometrics via OpenID Connect flows. 70% of passport requests are now made through Houwiyeti.
revision_notes: Confirmed via TECH5 and ID Tech Wire reporting: the Houwiyeti app (launched December 2023, public from January 2024) enables passwordless biometric login to Mauritanian eGov services using facial 1:1 matching (T5-OmniMatch) and liveness detection, via OpenID Connect. The '70% of passport requests' figure could not be corroborated in any source reviewed; official ANRPTS-sourced press reporting instead records passport requests as a minority share of total Houwiyeti transactions (c.63,000 of 554,000 remote services), so this statistic is dropped from the revised comments. Score of 2 (Yes) confirmed.
revised_comments: The Houwiyeti digital identity application, launched by the National Agency for Population Registry and Secure Titles (ANRPTS) in December 2023 and available to the public from January 2024, enables citizens to authenticate themselves digitally through facial biometric matching against their stored eID. Built on the TECH5 platform, the system uses OpenID Connect flows and liveness detection to replace password-based logins with biometric authentication for access to eGovernment services.

Definition: Whether authentication is possible through a centralized government portal or digital gateway
Comments: The e-ID/Houwiyeti system enables passwordless biometric login to the Mauritanian eGovernment portal. The system uses OpenID Connect flows and facial biometric verification (selfie against stored digital ID) for access to government online services. Over 622,000 document extracts were processed via the Houwiyeti platform in 2024. The Ijraati portal (2026) centralizes 800+ administrative procedures.
revision_notes: Confirmed - Houwiyeti enables passwordless biometric login to the Mauritanian eGovernment portal (TECH5/OpenID Connect). Newer evidence (We Are Tech, February 2026) confirms the government also launched the 'Ijraati' portal consolidating 800+ administrative procedures, feeding into the 'Khdamati' platform for full remote transaction completion. The '622,000 document extracts in 2024' figure was not corroborated in sources reviewed and is dropped from the revised comments.
revised_comments: Citizens can authenticate via a centralised government digital gateway. The Houwiyeti app provides passwordless biometric login to the Mauritanian eGovernment portal using facial verification against the stored digital ID. The government's 'Ijraati' portal, launched in February 2026, further centralises access to over 800 administrative procedures, with plans to integrate the most-used services into the 'Khdamati' platform for full remote completion.

Definition: Whether individuals can view their data held in the ID database and see how it has been accessed
Comments: Law No. 2017-020 grants data subjects the right to access their personal data held by organizations. The e-ID/Houwiyeti system uses a consent framework before sharing personal information, and biographic/biometric data is stored in an encrypted T5-Cryptograph on the citizen's phone. The Houwiyeti app also allows citizens to view and manage their own identity data and access document extracts digitally.
revision_notes: Confirmed - Law No. 2017-020 grants data subjects rights to access personal data; the Houwiyeti app allows users to view their own personal information and digital ID (eID) and verify documents issued by ANRPTS. The consent-based T5-Cryptograph architecture (data stored on the citizen's device) supports individual visibility/control of personal data.
revised_comments: Individuals can view their own data through the Houwiyeti mobile application, which displays the holder's digital identity (eID) and permits verification of documents issued by ANRPTS. Law No. 2017-020 on the protection of personal data separately grants data subjects a general right of access to personal data held by data controllers, alongside rights of rectification and erasure.

Definition: Whether the system enables Know Your Customer (KYC) packet collection for service provision, particularly financial services
Comments: The national ID card (and the e-ID system) enables KYC processes. The UNCDF (2020) confirms tiered-KYC requirements for account opening require a valid photo ID as minimum, and with ~90% ID penetration. Refugees need the national ID card to open bank accounts and obtain SIM cards. The e-ID system includes identity proofing (auto-ident) based on NIST standards, enabling e-KYC via the digital ID.
revision_notes: Confirmed. UNCDF (2020) documents tiered-KYC requiring at minimum a valid photo ID, with over 85% of the population holding an official photo ID. AFI/RFILC (2022) covers e-KYC and digital ID for refugee financial inclusion in Mauritania. The TECH5-built e-ID/Houwiyeti system supports NIST-based identity proofing suited to e-KYC, though direct evidence of a live e-KYC API integration specific to the digital (rather than physical) ID with banks was not found.
revised_comments: The national identity card underpins Know-Your-Customer processes for financial service providers: tiered-KYC rules require at minimum a valid photo ID to open an account, and over 85 percent of the population holds an official photo ID that can be used for this purpose. The TECH5-built digital identity platform additionally supports NIST-aligned identity proofing suited to electronic KYC use cases.

Definition: Whether the ID authority and system are subject to general oversight of the courts and judicial review
Value Name: Yes, but not specific to ID
Comments: Mauritania's constitution (Article 13) guarantees privacy of citizens. The Data Protection Law 2017-020 provides for criminal penalties and the APD has judicial/investigative powers. A magistrate from the Supreme Court is a member of the APD. Courts have jurisdiction over civil status disputes (late birth registration requires court judgment). However, no ID-specific judicial oversight mechanisms are identified in the evidence.
revision_notes: Confirmed. The Data Protection Authority (APD), established under Law No. 2017-020, includes a Supreme Court magistrate and a public prosecutor's office judge among its nine members (per its structure as described on French Wikipedia, updated March 2026), giving the judiciary a formal role in the data oversight body, though this is not an ID-specific judicial review mechanism. General courts retain jurisdiction over civil-status disputes such as late birth registration.
revised_comments: General judicial oversight applies to the ID system rather than an ID-specific review mechanism. Mauritania's Data Protection Authority (APD), created under Law No. 2017-020, includes a Supreme Court magistrate and a public prosecutor's office judge among its nine members, giving the judiciary representation in oversight of personal data processing, including biometric data. Ordinary courts retain jurisdiction over civil-status disputes, such as late birth registration, which requires a court judgment.

Definition: Whether the civil registration and digital ID systems are integrated
Comments: The ANRPTS manages both civil registration and ID issuance (birth/marriage certificates, ID cards, passports) through Centres d'Accueil des Citoyens (CAC). The SIGPTS (2020) integrates government structures. However, UNICEF estimated in 2015 that one third of children under 5 had no civil registration and HRW (2018) found significant gaps. The Houwiyeti platform processed 622,000 document extracts in 2024. Integration is partial, not fully interlinked with health sector birth notification.
revision_notes: Confirmed. ANRPTS manages both civil registration and ID issuance through the same Citizen Welcome Centres (CAC), and reports over 94% national ID coverage as of May 2025 (ID4Africa progress report). HRW's 2018 findings on registration gaps for children pre-date the current SIGPTS system and Houwiyeti roll-out, so the extent of remaining gaps under the current system is uncertain; integration through a single agency and shared registers is confirmed, but full interlinkage (e.g. automatic birth-to-ID pipelines) is not evidenced.
revised_comments: Civil registration and identity issuance are managed by the same agency, ANRPTS, through shared Citizen Welcome Centres and the integrated SIGPTS population register, giving partial integration between civil status records and the ID system. ANRPTS reported national ID coverage above 94 percent as of 2025. Full automatic linkage between birth registration and ID issuance is not documented.

Definition: Whether procedural rules for collection, storage, and sharing of ID-related personal data are publicly available and established
Comments: Law No. 2017-020 on personal data protection establishes rules for data processing and sharing, requiring consent and prohibiting incompatible secondary uses. The e-ID/Houwiyeti system includes a consent framework before sharing personal information (decentralized biometric authentication via T5-Cryptograph). The APD must authorize sensitive data transfers. However, the law has not fully come into force and complete data sharing rulebook for the digital ID system is still being developed.
revision_notes: Confirmed. Law No. 2017-020 establishes data processing/sharing rules and the APD's authorisation powers; the APD's own 2023-2026 strategic plan states its first strategic objective is to bring the 2017 law fully into force, indicating rules exist on paper but implementation/enforcement is still developing. The Houwiyeti/e-ID system separately includes an explicit consent framework before data sharing (TECH5).
revised_comments: Procedural rules on the collection, storage and sharing of personal data, including ID-related data, are set out in Law No. 2017-020, which requires consent for processing and gives the Data Protection Authority (APD) power to authorise transfers of sensitive data. The APD's 2023-2026 strategic plan identifies bringing the law into full operational force as its first priority, indicating that implementation of the data-sharing framework is still maturing. The Houwiyeti digital ID system separately applies a consent step before sharing a user's biometric and biographic data with relying parties.

Definition: Whether national data protection legislation exists and covers personal data linked to the ID system
Comments: Law No. 2017-020 on the protection of personal data was adopted by the National Assembly on 22 July 2017. It establishes the Personal Data Protection Authority (APD - Autorité de protection des données à caractère personnel) and grants data subjects rights of access, rectification, erasure, and objection. Mauritania also ratified the AU Malabo Convention in 2023 (15th state). Note: some sources indicate the 2017 law has not yet fully come into effect.
revision_notes: Confirmed. Law No. 2017-020 of 22 July 2017 on the protection of personal data established the APD and data subject rights.
revised_comments: National data protection legislation exists: Law No. 2017-020 of 22 July 2017 on the protection of personal data establishes rights of access, rectification, erasure and objection for data subjects, and covers personal data processing by public and private bodies. The law created the Data Protection Authority (APD) as national regulator.

Definition: Whether a Data Protection Authority or similar body regulates ID data collection and sharing by the ID system
Comments: The APD (Autorité de protection des données à caractère personnel) was created by Law No. 2017-020 as the national data protection regulator. It is empowered to authorize and control all personal data processing, investigate violations, and impose sanctions. It comprises nine members appointed by the head of state. In October 2024 it signed a cooperation MoU with Algeria's data protection authority and joined the Global Privacy Assembly in November 2024.
revision_notes: Confirmed. The APD, created by Law No. 2017-020, has authority to authorise and control all personal data processing, comprising nine members. Most recent developments: signed a data-protection cooperation MoU with Algeria's ANPP (October 2024) and joined the Global Privacy Assembly (November 2024), per French Wikipedia (updated March 2026).
revised_comments: A Data Protection Authority (APD - Autorité de protection des données à caractère personnel), created under Law No. 2017-020, regulates personal data processing nationally, including data collected by the ID system. It is empowered to authorise and control data processing by public and private bodies. In October 2024 the APD signed a cooperation memorandum with Algeria's data protection authority, and in November 2024 it joined the Global Privacy Assembly.

Definition: Whether the digital ID credential serves as legal proof of an individual's identity as codified in law
Comments: The biometric national ID card (Carte nationale d'identité biométrique) is an official legal document establishing the identity and nationality of the holder (ANRPTS). Under Decree No. 2012-030, the card is mandatory for all Mauritanians aged 16+ enrolled in the National Population Biometric Register. The National Identification Number (NIN) is required for most health, social services, and administrative functions.
revision_notes: Confirmed, and updated to reflect the current governing instrument. Decree No. 2021-138 of 3 August 2021 (superseding Decree No. 2012-030) establishes the 'Carte d'Identification' as the official secure national identity document, mandatory for all Mauritanians aged 16 and above holding a National Identification Number.
revised_comments: The biometric national identity card is the official legal document establishing a holder's identity and nationality. Decree No. 2021-138 of 3 August 2021 (superseding the earlier 2012 decree) governs its issuance and confirms the card is mandatory for all Mauritanians aged 16 and above who hold a National Identification Number from the National Biometric Population Register.

Definition: Whether formal legislation (act, law, regulation) governs digital identity including identification acts, digital ID laws, or equivalent legislation
Comments: A legal framework for the national ID system exists. Decree No. 2012-030 established the biometric national identity card and its issuance rules (replacing Decree No. 2000-028). Law No. 2011-003 governs civil registration (replacing Law 96-019). A new decree was adopted in July 2021 modernizing the ID card system. The ANRPTS operates under Ministry of Home Affairs supervision.
revision_notes: Confirmed. Decree No. 2021-138 of 3 August 2021 is the current legal instrument governing the national identity card, replacing Decree No. 2012-030. Civil registration is separately governed by Law No. 2011-003. ANRPTS operates under the Ministry of the Interior.
revised_comments: A formal legal framework governs the national identity system. Decree No. 2021-138 of 3 August 2021 establishes the secure contact/contactless-chip national identity card and its issuance procedures, replacing the earlier 2012 decree. Civil registration is separately governed by Law No. 2011-003, and the issuing agency, ANRPTS, operates under the supervision of the Ministry of the Interior.

Definition: Whether the Ministry of Finance has oversight of the financing and development of the digital ID system
Comments: A Ministry of Finance representative is a member of the APD (per Law 2017-020). The World Bank Digital and Human Capital Reform DPF (2021) includes digital transformation as a pillar with Ministry of Economic Affairs as implementing agency. However, explicit Ministry of Finance oversight specifically for the digital ID system budget and operations is not documented in available sources.
revision_notes: Evidence for Ministry of Finance oversight specifically of the digital ID system's financing is weak and indirect. The Finance ministry holds one of nine seats on the general Data Protection Authority (not the ID system itself), and the World Bank's 2021 DPF document treats digital transformation as one reform pillar with the Ministry of Economic Affairs (not Finance) as implementing agency. No source documents a dedicated MoF budget line or financial oversight role specific to the ID system. Flagged for human review rather than confirming 'Partial oversight'.
revised_comments: The extent of Ministry of Finance oversight of the digital ID system's financing and development is not clearly documented in available sources. A Ministry of Finance representative sits on the general Data Protection Authority board, and broader public-sector digital reforms have been financed through World Bank development policy operations, but no source establishes a specific budgetary oversight role for the Ministry of Finance over the ID system itself.

Definition: Whether the system collects biometric data and which modalities are collected (fingerprints, facial image, iris scans)
Comments: The national biometric system collects facial biometrics and fingerprints. The ANRPTS biometric national ID card includes photo (facial). The e-ID/Houwiyeti digital system (TECH5 platform, launched 2023) uses facial biometric 1:1 matching (T5-OmniMatch Face BioSDK) and liveness detection. ID cards issued after June 2022 have contactless capability with biometric chip. UNHCR cross-checks with national biometric database using fingerprints for refugees.
revision_notes: Confirmed - facial biometrics are captured via the TECH5-based Houwiyeti platform (T5-OmniMatch Face, T5-AirSnap Face, liveness detection); fingerprints are also collected as part of the National Biometric Population Register (used e.g. for UNHCR cross-checks of refugees). No specific evidence of iris scanning was found, but the scale groups facial capture under the same top code (3=Facial/Iris) regardless.
revised_comments: The national biometric system collects both fingerprints and facial images. Fingerprints are captured as part of the National Biometric Population Register underpinning the identity card. The Houwiyeti digital identity platform additionally captures a facial image for biometric 1:1 matching, using smartphone camera-based capture and liveness detection to prevent spoofing.

Definition: Whether identity records are stored in electronic/digital format versus paper-based records
Comments: The SIGPTS (Système Intégré de Gestion des Populations et des Titres Sécurisés) is a fully digital database system launched in 2020 managing population records and secure document issuance. Biometric data is stored electronically and cross-referenced with UNHCR systems. The Houwiyeti digital ID stores an encrypted T5-Cryptograph on users' phones backed by a central digital backend.
revision_notes: Confirmed. SIGPTS, launched 2020, is the digital population register underpinning ID issuance; Houwiyeti stores an encrypted digital credential on the user's device backed by a central digital system.
revised_comments: Identity records are held in electronic format. The Integrated Population and Secure Titles Management System (SIGPTS), launched in 2020, is a digital population register underpinning identity issuance nationwide, and the Houwiyeti application stores an encrypted digital identity credential on the holder's device, backed by a central digital system.

Definition: Whether the country has established or is actively developing a national digital identity system, including foundational ID systems that enable authentication across multiple services. Fully deployed means operational nationwide and accepting new registrations.
Comments: Mauritania has a fully deployed nationwide digital ID system. The ANRPTS (Agence nationale du registre des populations et des titres sécurisés) manages the national biometric system (SIGPTS - Système Intégré de Gestion des Populations et des Titres Sécurisés) launched in 2020, issuing biometric national identity cards nationwide. Over 94% population coverage reported as of 2025. The Houwiyeti digital ID app launched in 2023 further extends the system.
revision_notes: Confirmed. ID4Africa progress report (May 2025) states Mauritania has enrolled over 94% of the population under the biometric system launched in 2020 (SIGPTS), a foundational, nationally deployed system, satisfying 'fully deployed nationwide' even though the newer Houwiyeti mobile digital-ID layer built on this foundation was still described as a 'pilot' in UNDP's August 2024 blog. Year updated to reflect the most recent coverage figure.
revised_comments: Mauritania operates a fully deployed, nationwide foundational identity system. The National Agency for Population Registry and Secure Titles (ANRPTS) has enrolled more than 94 percent of the population under the biometric system (SIGPTS) launched in 2020, issuing biometric national identity cards. This foundational system underpins the Houwiyeti mobile digital identity application, launched in December 2023, which extends authentication and document services to citizens' smartphones.

Definition: Whether the digital ID system is designed to be interoperable across government agencies and with other systems through APIs or data exchange protocols
Comments: The SIGPTS integrates all government structures involved in the issuance of ID documents (ANRPTS, 2020). The e-ID/Houwiyeti system uses an Identity Provider (IdP) backend with OpenID Connect flows enabling passwordless login to the Mauritanian eGovernment portal. The solution was contributed to MOSIP (Modular Open Source Identity Platform). Houwiyeti enables access to multiple government services without visiting offices.
revision_notes: Confirmed. SIGPTS integrates the government structures involved in issuing ID documents; the e-ID/Houwiyeti backend uses OpenID Connect for interoperable authentication with the eGovernment portal, and its source code was contributed to MOSIP.
revised_comments: The digital ID system is designed for cross-agency interoperability. The SIGPTS population register integrates the government structures involved in issuing identity documents, and the Houwiyeti/e-ID backend uses OpenID Connect-based authentication, enabling passwordless access to multiple eGovernment services from a single credential. The underlying solution's source code has been contributed to the MOSIP open-source identity platform.

Definition: Whether credential is accepted or mandatory for opening bank accounts and accessing financial services
Comments: The national ID card is accepted (but not universally mandatory) for banking and financial services. UNCDF (2020) confirms tiered-KYC requires minimum a valid photo ID for account opening. Refugees require the national ID card specifically to open bank accounts. The AFI/RFILC report confirms the national ID enables bank account access. No evidence of mandatory ID requirement for all banking transactions across all institutions.
revision_notes: Confirmed. UNCDF (2020) documents tiered-KYC requiring at minimum a valid photo ID to open an account; AFI/RFILC (2022) confirms refugees require the national ID card specifically to open bank accounts. No evidence of a universal mandatory ID requirement across all institutions/products.
revised_comments: The national identity card is accepted, though not universally mandatory, for opening bank accounts and accessing financial services. Tiered Know-Your-Customer rules require at minimum a valid photo ID to open a basic account, and refugees specifically require the national ID card to open bank accounts and register SIM cards.

Definition: Whether credentials are issued free of charge
Comments: A fee of 1,000 ouguiya (approximately USD 5 / CAD 5) must be paid to obtain the biometric national identity card. This fee was introduced with the biometric card (the previous version was free). NGOs noted this fee represents a barrier for poorer citizens. The fee structure has not been reported as removed or waived as of the latest available evidence.
revision_notes: Confirmed a fee applies. IRB/ecoi.net sources (2015, citing 2012-2013 reporting) document a 1,000 ouguiya (~US$5) issuance fee. The newer Decree No. 2021-138 (Article 4) continues to require payment of fees for establishment, replacement or renewal 'fixés par les textes en vigueur' for the current card, confirming the credential remains fee-based, though the current exact fee amount was not located in the sources reviewed.
revised_comments: Identity credentials are not issued free of charge. A fee has applied to the biometric national identity card since its introduction, historically reported at around 1,000 ouguiya (approximately US$5). Decree No. 2021-138 of 3 August 2021, which governs the current identity card, continues to require payment of an issuance, replacement or renewal fee set by the regulations in force.

Definition: Whether the digital ID is recognized or interoperable across borders through regional agreements or travel documents
Value Name: Recognized in some regional contexts (e.g., ECOWAS travel)
Comments: Mauritania re-entered ECOWAS trading structures in 2017 but is not a full political member and did not adopt free movement provisions. Mauritania has bilateral free movement agreements with Senegal. Citizens of Côte d'Ivoire, Gambia, Mali and Niger can enter Mauritania visa-free with a passport. Mauritania is not part of the WURI ECOWAS ID interoperability programme (which covers Benin, Burkina Faso, Côte d'Ivoire, Guinea, Niger, Togo). Some regional recognition exists but no formal cross-border interoperability established.
revision_notes: Confirmed. Mauritania is an ECOWAS founding member (1975) but withdrew from full ECOWAS political integration in 2000 and has an ambiguous relationship with ECOWAS free movement provisions (Chatham House, 2019). It is not among the six countries (Benin, Burkina Faso, Côte d'Ivoire, Guinea, Niger, Togo) participating in the World Bank/ECOWAS WURI identity interoperability programme, confirming recognition is limited/regional rather than formally interoperable.
revised_comments: Regional recognition of the Mauritanian identity credential is limited rather than formally interoperable. Mauritania was a founding ECOWAS member but maintains a distinct, more distant relationship with the bloc's free-movement provisions, and it is not one of the six countries (Benin, Burkina Faso, Côte d'Ivoire, Guinea, Niger, Togo) participating in the World Bank-backed West Africa Unique Identification for Regional Integration and Inclusion (WURI) programme for cross-border ID interoperability. Bilateral free-movement arrangements exist with some neighbouring states, such as Senegal.

Definition: Age in years at which an individual becomes eligible to register for digital ID
Comments: Under Decree No. 2012-030, the biometric national identity card is mandatory for all Mauritanians aged 16 years and older enrolled in the National Population Biometric Register. The civil registration process starting in 2011 covers all citizens, but the ID card enrollment age threshold is 16+. No evidence found of mandatory enrollment below age 16.
revision_notes: The original Value Code (1, '>17') did not match the scale definition given the evidence originally cited (mandatory age 16 falls within the '10-17' bracket, code 2), and newer evidence changes the picture further. Decree No. 2021-138 (3 August 2021), Article 3, states the identity card is mandatory from age 16, but any citizen aged 6 or above may apply for one voluntarily ('Tout citoyen âgé de six (6) ans peut obtenir à sa demande une Carte d'Identification'). As the variable measures the age of eligibility (not the mandatory age, captured by a separate variable), the correct code is 3 (6-10 years), reflecting the voluntary eligibility floor of age 6.
revised_comments: Individuals become eligible to apply for the national identity card from age 6, under Decree No. 2021-138 of 3 August 2021, which permits any citizen aged six or above to request a card voluntarily. The card becomes mandatory at age 16, at which point every citizen must hold a National Identification Number-linked identity card.

Definition: Whether registration for digital ID is mandatory, optional, or mandatory for specific groups
Comments: Under Decree No. 2012-030, the national identity card is mandatory for all Mauritanians aged 16 years and older enrolled in the National Population Biometric Register. The 2016 joint Interior-Education Ministry memorandum required biometric registration for school enrollment and national exams. Civil registration (birth certificates, NIN) is required for most health and social services.
revision_notes: Confirmed and updated to the current governing decree. Decree No. 2021-138 (Article 3) confirms the identity card is mandatory for all Mauritanians aged 16 and above holding a National Identification Number. HRW (2018) documents that civil registration/NIN is separately a practical requirement for school enrolment and national examinations, though implementation gaps affect poorer families.
revised_comments: Registration is mandatory for all citizens. Decree No. 2021-138 of 3 August 2021 confirms the national identity card is compulsory for every Mauritanian aged 16 or above who holds a National Identification Number from the biometric population register. Civil registration and the resulting identification number are also a practical requirement for school enrolment and national examinations, though implementation gaps have historically affected poorer families' ability to comply.

Definition: Whether credential is accepted or mandatory for accessing public healthcare services
Comments: The NIN/national ID is required for most health and social services per HRW (2018). The CNAM (Caisse Nationale d'Assurance Maladie) uses national ID for health insurance registration. The joint SDG Fund programme in Guidimakha used ID documents for health insurance affiliation of disabled people. However, no evidence of strictly mandatory national ID requirement for all healthcare access; ID is accepted but not always mandatory in all health settings.
revision_notes: Confirmed via a more direct primary source than originally cited. Mauritania's official procedures portal (procedures.gov.mr, Ministry of Health, last updated December 2023) confirms that CNASS health-insurance membership applications require an identity document (national ID card, passport, or birth certificate for citizens; residence card or bilateral-agreement ID for migrants; refugee/asylum documentation for refugees) - i.e. accepted, but the ID is one of several acceptable identity documents rather than an exclusively mandatory national ID. The original CNAM-specific claim was not corroborated and has been replaced with the verified CNASS procedure.
revised_comments: Identity documentation is required to register for public health insurance, but the national ID card is one of several acceptable proofs of identity rather than an exclusively mandatory credential. Mauritania's official administrative procedures portal confirms that National Social Insurance Fund (CNASS) health-insurance enrolment requires presentation of a national identity card, passport, or birth certificate for citizens, with equivalent alternative documents accepted for migrants and refugees.

Chapter Details: The architecture, governance, functionality and uptake of government digital identity systems and credentials. 30 variables in 5 sections. Contains latest available data. Data collection by Perplexity from a variety of sources.
Definition: Whether non-nationals including refugees, asylum seekers, and permanent residents are eligible to register
Comments: Refugees (but not asylum-seekers) are eligible for the national ID card in Mauritania. ANRPTS began biometrically enrolling urban refugees in October 2014 to issue national refugee documentation. Only recognized refugees qualify; asylum-seekers receive UNHCR ID cards only. Refugees require the national ID card to open bank accounts and obtain SIM cards. Non-citizen residents can apply for a residence card (carte de séjour).
revision_notes: Confirmed.
